newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian rebels rebuff peace proposal.
newsitem.headline: Colombian rebels rebuff peace proposal.

text.p: Leaders of Colombia's top leftist guerrilla group have poured cold water on President Ernesto Samper's call for unconditional peace talks, saying they have no interest in negotiating with "an illegitimate government."

The embattled Samper, severely weakened by charges he used drug money to finance his 1994 election campaign, called for the talks last Friday in a statement that said the government recognised Colombia's rebels as a legitimate political force.

But leaders of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), the country's largest and oldest rebel group, rebuffed the peace initiative. "The FARC has said that it cannot and will not sit down with an illegtimate government," Raul Reyes, one of the group's maximum leaders, said in an interview late on Sunday from Costa Rica with Colombia's TV Hoy news programme.
Branding the government "nefarious," he said that it was "questioned on all sides and only looking for breathing space by talking about a peace that it has never wanted to make."

FARC military leaders Luciano Marin Arango, whose nom de guerrre is Ivan Marquez, and Jorge Briceno Suarez, popularly known as "Mono Jojoy," were equally dismissive of Samper's proposal in a two-way radio conversation last Friday that was intercepted and taped by military intelligence. Excerpts from the 52-minute conversation, whose authenticity was confirmed to Reuters by military intelligence sources, were published in Monday's edition of the weekly news magazine Semana.

In it, Marquez said he was cautiously optimistic about the appointment of Gilberto Echeverri Mejia, a civilian business leader who was sworn in as defence minister on Friday with a vow to make the pursuit of peace his top priority. But he added that "while Samper has appointed a serious guy, the government itself isn't serious."
When Samper unveiled a peace plan in May 1995, the FARC and National Liberation Army (ELN) responded by launching a bloody offensive in which more than 150 people were killed and hundreds injured.

There has been no such response to the latest overture, but analysts say both rebel groups, which were founded in the mid-1960s, are stronger than ever and unlikely to engage in serious peace talks unless the government makes substantial concessions in advance of any face-to-face bargaining.

Such concessions, which rebel leaders say must include the demilitarization of vast tracts of Colombian territory, are something the notoriously weak Samper government is in no position to wrest from powerful military leaders.

Enrique Santos Calderon, deputy director of Bogota's El Tiempo newspaper and one of Colombia's leading columnists, said there was no reason to hope that Latin America's longest running guerrilla war, which has taken tens of thousands of lives over more than three decades, will end any time soon.

"This is not only because the guerrillas have said they have no interest in talking with a government they consider unworthy," Santos said, "but because they're going through an open period of military and territorial expansion that makes them even more unwilling to negotiate."
